title: The May 2026 budget forecasts net overseas migration falling to 245,000 in 2026–27 and 225,000 a year from 2027–28
oneLiner: The number is already heading back to its pre-pandemic range without a cap.
body: Budget forecasts put net overseas migration at 295,000 in 2025–26, 245,000 in 2026–27 and 225,000 a year thereafter, roughly the level of the decade before the pandemic. Treasury's long-run assumption is about 235,000. A cap of 200,000 would therefore bind by 25,000 to 45,000 a year on current forecasts.
contextBackground: Forecasts of net migration have been wrong before, in both directions, which is the main reason sceptics do not take the glide path at face value.
contextDisagreement: Agreed as the budget's figure. Disputed is whether it will be met: one line of commentary says the long-run forecast is too low, another that the decline is already visible in the data.

otherClaim.title: Net overseas migration should be held below 200,000 a year

claimItself.title: Net overseas migration should be held below 200,000 a year
claimItself.oneLiner: Whether the federal government should cap net arrivals below the levels of the past decade and well below the post-pandemic peak.
claimItself.body: Net overseas migration is arrivals minus departures of people who stay, or leave, for at least twelve months. It averaged just over 200,000 a year in the decade before the pandemic and exceeded 500,000 in 2022–23. The proposal is a cap of 200,000, which would require the government to manage the student, temporary-work and permanent programs together to hit it.

otherClaim.title: The 2022–23 surge largely reflected students and temporary workers returning after two years of closed borders

claimItself.title: The 2022–23 surge largely reflected students and temporary workers returning after two years of closed borders
claimItself.oneLiner: Two cohorts arrived in one year because none arrived in the two before.
claimItself.body: Net migration was negative in 2020–21. When borders reopened, the students and temporary workers who would have come across two or three years arrived together, and departures were low because few had been in the country long enough to leave. The Centre for Population's projections show net migration falling back towards its long-run level without any change in policy.
